Caitlin covered the point I was going to make about TROY and Ithaca; I went about it this way: 

As a New Yorker who has spent a decent amount of time in all parts of the state, I first thought about the two cities (not townships) in my state, but wondering, because (a) TROY is east of Ithaca, but nowhere near it, and (b) TROY is actually ENE of Ithaca, which could be the basis of a three-letter answer in some other puzzle.  

But then, I thought, wow, maybe the clue is referring to the original Ithaca and TROY.  So I looked at a map, and found that the exact same points are valid for those two:  they're nowhere near each other, and TROY is ENE of Ithaca.  Plus, there's a sea between themm.

So after the solve, I looked for TROY, Michigan, and then searched to see if there was an Ithaca, Michigan.  Apparently, there is, but TROY is southeast of Ithaca.

So who knows which ones the constructor meant.

Note to Caitlin:

Serena won all four grand slam events consecutively over two different seasons each time; that is the essence of this achievement.  Thus, she held all four titles at the same time, but they were contested over the course of two seasons.

The tennis season is practically all year, but there is a break of about a month between late November and early January.  This break delineates each tennis season, which always falls out entirely within one calendar year.

Win all four grand slam titles in one year (one season), it's a grand slam.  Will all four grand slam titles in a row, but over two years (i.e. two seasons), it's a Serena slam.

And there are those who say that the phrase "Serena slam" only refers to the times Serena did it, although she's not the only one who has.

I think I've found the crossword-solving analogy I've been wanting. A funny moment in R.F. Kuang’s Taipei Story involves the narrator thinking about her conversational challenges: 
 
“The problem was that I never wanted to know whether someone had siblings and pets, or how much they had disliked growing up in the suburbs. I wanted to know what they would do if they were a gladiator in the Colosseum, and the Colosseum was flooded, and they had to fight a shark.”

I feel this way about crosswords. I enjoy a pets-and-siblings puzzle (and today’s puzzle had lots more zing than that, so please know I'm speaking more generally!). I just so love a flooded-Colosseum-with-shark puzzle. And that's what I hope for at the end of the week: the thrill of "I didn’t see that coming!"; moments of dumbfounded "wait, what?!"; lots of extra-sneaky misdirections; a bit of "OMG, what to do now??" I didn’t experience that today, despite some lively fill.

Definitely plenty of fun to be had with this puzzle, and I'm not disparaging its skookum constructor. And this isn’t about bragging or a diss to newer solvers, though I feel blue knowing it may be read that way by some. But what I'm trying to get at is a kind of frisson-filled encounter that Friday and Saturday puzzles are best suited to offer. NYT, please do keep giving us fresh, well-crafted puzzles like today’s. But on the weekends, please flood the Colosseum and add a shark!

I came late to Friday night/Saturday's puzzle with its constructor's revelations on 'how the sausage is made', and the reply facility there just closed. But I did want to add my 2c. So here I am:
It is  disappointing to watch people continue the outsourcing of the actual creation of the puzzle. I'm not saying that I want the setter to press their own wood pulp into paper to create a "handmade, artisanal, non-GMO" puzzle. 
But offloading the creation and maintenance of word lists to the machines means the loss  of the setter's individuality: e.g., they love tennis and folklore, know nothing about football but adore Mozart, speak Latin or are Latino. All that will be reflected in  their clues and fill. Or would have been, until they let the machines take over the 'tedium' of creating and curating word lists. What is the point of enlisting new setters in all their particularity if their 'own' puzzle is comprised of pap from the same trough of gruel?
I value that human element and am sorry and anģry to watch that spiky individuality being covered by a layer of cement autofill. 🤨

It's a critical thinking issue.  Some of the relative newbies are thrilled that we get easy late-week puzzles, because they can say they finished them.  But they've missed the experience of longtime solvers who, forty years ago, regularly faced stone-faced stumpers (and without a clear progression to indicate when they were coming).  All they could do is look at the answer key the next day, and if they didn't get why an answer worked, they'd better have had a flesh-and-bones friend who did.  No internet, no comment section.

But what's the fun of climbing Bunker Hill and acting as if you've climbed Everest?  I guarantee that with nothing new to challenge them, there won't be any forty-year-long solvers thirty years from now.
As righteous as it is harsh.

Welp…accidentally hit submit about halfway through typing that last comment (something that has happened to me a few times here lately).

But anyway, you can probably see where I was going with that: during the last couple years, as puzzles have gotten easier and lots of newer solvers have started solving them, this comments section has…changed.

For one thing, lots of the newer solvers tend to get very mad about “too easy” commentary, in part because they seem to take such comments as personal insults (not realizing that those comments are not directed *at* them, but toward other solvers for whom the current puzzles are simply way too easy).

Also, lots of people who are newer to this forum, feeling buoyed by their burgeoning crossword-solving hobby and being unaccustomed to the forum’s discursive patterns, come out righteously against  “too easy” complainers, from a quasi-moralistic perspective that seems to be inspired by a more generic opposition to negativity in internet comments sections (than anything specific to the NYT Crossword).
@Andy Phelps keep posting.
Mass media has learned that there is a gold mine in exploiting Dunning-Kruger.
